ety.text: Likely from Proto-West Germanic *furhisti. The shape of the word in Latin recalls the adjective agrestis. Alternatively, a shortening of an expression like silva *forestis, the latter an unattested adjective derived from forās (“outside”) or forum (“court”) + -est(r)is (adjective ending). In the former case the etymological sense would perhaps be “forest outside of public use” and in the latter case “forest belonging to the court”.

ety.text: From morphological reanalysis of pauper, originally a third-declension one-termination adjective. Probably inflected initially as pauper, paupera, pauperum, after the model of Classical Latin adjectives such as miser, misera, miserum. The change in declension would be facilitated by the ambiguous masculine nominative singular form. Then the oblique forms would in turn provide the analogical basis for a new masculine nominative singular pauperus: however, this form is unattested in ancient Latin and occurs rarely even in medieval times. In contrast, some of the oblique forms are attested early…

ety.text: The first part is from vic-, vicis (“alternation, turn”) and the final part is from the adverb-forming suffix -tim (etymologically the adverbial accusative of the i-stem abstract noun suffix *-tis), but the details of its formation are unclear. The -ss- would be expected to go back to original *-t-t- or *-d-t-, hence pre-forms such as *vici-dtim (a compound with the root of dō, dare, dedī, datum) or *vici-cessim (a compound with the root of cēdō, cēdere, cessī, cessum) have been proposed. Compare anteclassical vicissātim.
